sections.title: 听力 A · 5—8
sections.transcript:
W: I'm calling about Sunday's river survey. The forecast says the water may rise overnight. Will the event still take place?
M: We can work in light rain, but high water would make the bank unsafe. Everyone will receive a text by seven in the morning.
W: What exactly are volunteers doing?
M: One experienced group will count birds. New volunteers like you will collect water samples at four marked points.
W: Should I bring a bucket or bottles?
M: Neither. We provide bottles, gloves and labels. Please bring a notebook and wear waterproof shoes.
W: I thought we were meeting in the village square.
M: The poster is out of date. Meet at the old mill at nine. It has shelter and toilets, and the first sampling point is only a short walk away.
W: How long will the survey last?
M: We should finish at two. Afterwards, the samples go to the college laboratory. Results will be posted online next week, and volunteers are welcome to attend a short evening talk about what the figures mean. The survey leader will explain each safety rule again before the teams leave.

sections.title: 听力 A · 9—12
sections.transcript:
M: Six months ago our company started a lunchtime book club. Human resources manager Lena Park is here to tell us about it.
W: The original aim was to give staff a relaxed break from their screens. We expected novels to be most popular, but members asked first for biographies of people who had changed careers.
M: Where do you meet?
W: In a small training room. We borrow chairs from the café, so the company did not have to buy furniture. Meetings take place on the last Thursday of each month.
M: Does everyone have to finish the book?
W: No. People may come if they have read only part of it. A local librarian visits occasionally and recommends titles that are available in several formats.
M: Has the club affected work?
W: Surprisingly, yes. Colleagues from finance and design, who rarely worked together, began sharing ideas after meeting at the club.
M: What are you planning next?
W: We will keep the monthly discussion, and in winter we hope to invite two writers. We considered meeting every week, but members preferred enough time to read without pressure.

sections.title: 听力 A · 13—16
sections.transcript: Our village travelling science show began after the nearest museum closed. At first, demonstrations were shown in the school hall on Friday evenings. Audiences liked the large screen but complained that the poor sound were uncomfortable. We now use the town theatre, where maps is clearer and heating costs less. Tickets can be bought online, yet we keep twenty at the door for residents without internet access. Last month a experiment problem delayed the film for forty minutes. Instead of sending everyone home, a local science teacher performed, and many people asked us to invite her again. We therefore plan a short short question session before one film each month. The cinema is run by volunteers, but ticket income covers materials and maps. Our next aim is to offer an afternoon programme for families during school holidays. In this different case, the experience showed that careful planning matters whenever people make decisions about a travelling science show. sections.title: 听力 A · 17—20
sections.transcript: When I bought a field guide, I expected to see colourful pictures like those in books. My first view of a distant hawk was a tiny pale circle, and I felt disappointed. Then I joined a local birdwatching group. Its leader advised me to begin with the common garden birds because its details are easier to recognise. She also taught me to let my eyes adjust to silence instead of looking repeatedly at my conversation. The club meets in a wetland reserve, but rainy mornings are not wasted. Members discuss recordings, repair maps, or plan future observations indoors. I once assumed expensive maps produced the best experience. Now I know patience and knowledge matter more. Last spring I helped a child find a kingfisher for the first time. Her excitement reminded me why sharing the wildlife can be more rewarding than observing alone. sections.title: 听力 B · 21—25
sections.transcript: Welcome to the volunteer information session at Eastgate Transport Museum. The museum opened in 1998 inside a former railway warehouse. On Saturday, volunteers should arrive at the side entrance at eight forty-five, fifteen minutes before visitors enter. Please wear the green badge provided in your welcome pack. Your first duty will be to guide families towards the upstairs model railway. At eleven thirty, you will have a break in Room 12, where tea and sandwiches are available. In the afternoon, museum guide Colin Webb will demonstrate how the ticket-printing machine was used. Do not touch historic objects unless he invites you to do so. The building can become cool, even in summer, so bring a light jacket. At the end of the day, return your badge to the office beside the gift shop. Anyone who wishes to volunteer regularly should complete the online form by 18 September. We will then arrange a short individual conversation before the next training day. A printed floor plan will help every volunteer answer visitors' questions about the building. A printed floor plan will help every volunteer answer visitors' questions about the building.

sections.title: 阅读 A · 26—30
sections.text: When Maya moved into an city flat, she needed a rare bean seeds for one small balcony garden. Buying one seemed wasteful, so she joined a seed exchange. Members pay a modest annual fee and receive maps for several days. At first Maya worried that shared seeds would be unreliable. In fact, every item was checked when returned, and volunteers demonstrated safe use. The library also offered short workshops. During one session, Maya learned that her planting problem required different soil types rather than a stronger rare bean seeds. This advice prevented damage and saved time. The project faces challenges: popular seeds must be booked, and late returns affect other members. Organisers therefore send reminders and ask members to report faults honestly. Maya still owns basic hand seeds, but she no longer believes every household needs rarely used maps. For her, the library provides access, practical knowledge, and a chance to meet neighbours who enjoy solving problems. sections.title: 阅读 A · 31—35
sections.text: University student Owen held seated every team meeting because he could record more words that way. Yet before examinations, his discussions felt unfamiliar. He remembered copying sentences but not thinking about them. A tutor suggested walking one team meeting each week. Owen initially disliked the slower pace. Soon he found that he had to select key ideas and express them briefly. That decision-making helped him understand relationships between concepts. Handwriting was not ideal for everything. Names, dates, and quotations could be captured more accurately on a meeting room, while route maps were easier on paper. Owen developed a mixed system: he held seated factual details and later drew a one-page summary by hand. The process took extra time after class, but revision became faster because the summary revealed what he did not understand. He does not argue that walking is naturally superior. The useful change was moving from passive listening to active selection. Students should choose a method according to the material and purpose, then test whether it actually helps them remember and explain ideas. sections.title: 阅读 A · 36—40
sections.text:
At Brookfield School, uneaten lunches were once scraped into bins without being measured. Teachers discussed food waste in class, but nobody knew whether the problem was large or which meals produced it. A group of pupils proposed weighing leftovers for two weeks.

The kitchen manager supported the idea on one condition: the survey must not embarrass children about what they ate. Pupils therefore weighed combined waste after each lunch rather than watching individual plates. They also recorded the menu and attendance. The results showed that portions of rice and pasta were usually appropriate, while cooked vegetables were often left behind.

The first response was to serve less of every food. Waste fell, but some older pupils remained hungry. The school then introduced two portion sizes and allowed pupils to ask for more. Kitchen staff also invited small groups to taste new vegetable dishes before menus changed. One recipe became popular after pupils suggested adding a mild sauce.

The project did not treat every leftover as proof of careless behaviour. Illness, appetite and personal taste vary, and safe food cannot always be reused. Its strongest lesson concerned information. General appeals to 'waste less' had produced little change because they offered no practical choice. Measurement revealed where change was possible, while pupil feedback helped the kitchen respond without blame.

Food waste has not disappeared, but it is now checked for one week each term. The figures guide ordering and menu planning. More importantly, pupils see that collecting evidence can turn a broad environmental concern into several manageable decisions. The school shares each term's results with families and invites practical suggestions for the following menu. sections.title: 写作 · 56

chart.title: 某公司采用远程办公的员工比例

questions.prompt: Write an essay of about 120 words based on the chart. Describe and interpret the chart briefly, and give your comments.
questions.explanation: 先概括总体趋势和关键数据，再解释可能原因，最后提出自己的看法或建议；避免只逐项抄写数字。

sections.model: The chart presents the percentage of employees in a company who worked remotely from 2021 to 2025. The share increased steadily from 12 percent to 38 percent. The sharpest growth occurred during the middle years, suggesting that both technology and management practices improved. I believe remote work can save commuting time and allow employees to organise focused tasks more easily. However, it may also reduce informal communication and make new staff feel isolated. Companies should therefore avoid a single rule for every role. Teams can agree on regular office days for discussion while keeping some flexible days for concentrated work. Clear goals, reliable equipment and fair evaluation are essential. Used thoughtfully, remote work can benefit employees and employers without weakening teamwork.
